name: atmospheric-entry
description: Simplified pre-parachute atmospheric entry dynamics for blunt capsules. Integrates a 2D planet-centered entry-plane model with gravity, drag, and in-plane lift.

limits: Fixed Cd and L/D per vehicle
Stops at parachute deployment altitude instead of splashdown

sliders.s2_vehicle: Vehicle preset index: 0 Dragon, 1 Gemini, 2 Apollo CM, 3 Orion
sliders.s2_gamma: Entry flight-path angle magnitude in degrees below local horizontal
sliders.s2_bank: Bank angle in degrees; in-plane lift scales with cos(bank)
sliders.s2_g_limit: Crew-load threshold used to define the corridor

functions: entryVehicleName(), entryVehicleMission(), entryVehicleMass(), entryVehicleArea(), entryVehicleCd(), entryVehicleBeta(), entryVehicleLD(), entryVehicleSpeed(), entryVehicleNominalGamma(), entryChuteAlt()

entry interface.markdown: The conventional altitude where atmospheric entry begins, about $120$ km ($400{,}000$ ft); entry speed and flight-path angle are quoted here.
entry interface.prompt: Explain what entry interface is and why entry conditions are specified there.

ballistic coefficient.markdown: $\beta = \dfrac{m}{C_D A}$ — mass per unit drag area. A high $\beta$ slices deeper into the atmosphere before slowing; a low $\beta$ decelerates high up where the air is thin.
ballistic coefficient.prompt: Explain the ballistic coefficient and how it changes where and how hard a vehicle decelerates.

scale height.markdown: The height $H$ over which air density falls by a factor of $e$: $\rho = \rho_0 e^{-h/H}$. For Earth's lower atmosphere $H \approx 7$–$8.5$ km.
scale height.prompt: Explain the atmospheric scale height and what the exponential atmosphere model assumes.

exponential atmosphere.markdown: The model $\rho(h) = \rho_0\, e^{-h/H}$: density falls by a constant factor for every scale height $H$ of altitude. It follows from hydrostatic balance at constant temperature.
exponential atmosphere.prompt: Explain the exponential atmosphere model and where it breaks down.

stagnation point.markdown: The point on the vehicle's nose where the oncoming flow is brought to rest. Pressure and heating peak there.
stagnation point.prompt: Explain the stagnation point and why heating is highest there.

bow shock.markdown: A curved shock wave standing ahead of a blunt body in hypersonic flow. The gas crossing it is compressed and heated to thousands of kelvin, and a blunt nose keeps that hot layer detached from the surface.
bow shock.prompt: Explain the detached bow shock and why blunt capsules survive entry better than sharp ones.

adiabatic compression.markdown: Compression too fast for heat to leave, so the work done on the gas all goes into its temperature. Entry heating is mostly this compression in the shock layer — not friction.
adiabatic compression.prompt: Explain why entry heating comes from adiabatic compression rather than friction.

skip entry.markdown: An entry that uses lift to climb back out of the atmosphere after a first dip, then re-enters. It spreads the heating and deceleration over two passes and extends range.
skip entry.prompt: Explain skip entry, why a capsule might skip, and when an unplanned skip is dangerous.

entry corridor.markdown: The band of flight-path angles that works. Too shallow and the vehicle skips out or lingers; too steep and deceleration or heating exceeds what crew and heat shield can take.
entry corridor.prompt: Explain the entry corridor and what sets its steep and shallow limits.

flight-path angle.markdown: $\gamma$ — the angle between the velocity and the local horizontal. Negative means descending; entry angles are typically a few degrees below horizontal.
flight-path angle.prompt: Explain the flight-path angle and why a few degrees makes such a difference at entry.

lift-to-drag ratio.markdown: $L/D$ — how much lift the vehicle makes per unit drag. Even a capsule's small $L/D$ (about $0.3$) is enough to steer by rolling the lift vector.
lift-to-drag ratio.prompt: Explain the lift-to-drag ratio and how a capsule uses a small L/D to control its entry.

bank angle.markdown: The roll of the lift vector about the velocity. Banking tilts lift away from vertical, trading altitude control for sideways steering.
bank angle.prompt: Explain how a capsule uses bank angle to control its entry without changing its shape.

heat shield.markdown: The protective layer on the vehicle's forward face. Ablative shields char and erode, carrying heat away with the material they shed.
heat shield.prompt: Explain how ablative heat shields protect entry vehicles.

g-load.markdown: Deceleration expressed in multiples of Earth gravity $g_0 = 9.81$ m/s². Crewed entries aim to stay within a few g.
g-load.prompt: Explain g-load during entry and what limits a crewed vehicle can tolerate.

dynamic pressure.markdown: $q = \tfrac12 \rho v^2$ — the pressure scale of the oncoming flow. Drag is $D = q\, C_D A$.
dynamic pressure.prompt: Explain dynamic pressure and how it sets drag and structural loads.

drag coefficient.markdown: $C_D$ — the dimensionless factor in $D = \tfrac12 \rho v^2 C_D A$ that captures how the shape resists the flow.
drag coefficient.prompt: Explain the drag coefficient and how shape changes it.

terminal velocity.markdown: The speed where drag equals weight, so the vehicle stops accelerating: $v_t = \sqrt{\dfrac{2 m g}{\rho\, C_D A}}$. It rises with altitude as the air thins.
terminal velocity.prompt: Explain terminal velocity and why it depends on altitude.

Mach number.markdown: Speed divided by the local speed of sound. Entry begins at Mach $25$ or more; shocks form wherever the flow is supersonic.
Mach number.prompt: Explain the Mach number and what changes as a vehicle slows through the speed of sound.

LEO.markdown: Orbits roughly $160$–$2{,}000$ km up. A return from LEO starts entry at about $7.8$ km/s, slower than a return from the Moon at about $11$ km/s.
LEO.prompt: Explain why returning from low Earth orbit is gentler than returning from the Moon.

ODE.markdown: An equation for how quantities change with one variable (here time). The entry model is a set of ODEs for speed, flight-path angle and altitude, integrated step by step.
ODE.prompt: Explain the ordinary differential equations behind a point-mass entry model and how they are solved numerically.

parachute.markdown: Deployed only after the vehicle has slowed well below the speed of sound; a small drogue usually stabilises and slows it before the main chutes open.
parachute.prompt: Explain why parachutes deploy late in entry and what the drogue chute is for.

Apollo.markdown: NASA's crewed lunar programme (1961–1972). Its capsules returned from the Moon at about $11$ km/s and flew guided entries using a small lift-to-drag ratio.
Apollo.prompt: Explain how Apollo capsules re-entered from the Moon.

Orion.markdown: NASA's crew capsule for Artemis. Its $5$ m heat shield is the largest flown on a crewed capsule, and it returns from the Moon at about $11$ km/s.
Orion.prompt: Explain how Orion re-enters the atmosphere on a lunar return.
